F1.quote: Vesuvius Challenge is an open science research organization reading the carbonized Herculaneum scrolls without unrolling them.

F3.quote: Resurrecting an ancient library from the ashes of a volcano. Buried in 79 AD, now being revealed.
F3.claim: its motto: an ancient library resurrected from a volcano's ashes, buried in 79 AD and now being revealed
F3.lineage: the scrolls: the library of the Villa of the Papyri, carbonized in 79 AD

F4.quote: Vesuvius erupts, burying a villa and its library of papyrus scrolls under twenty meters of ash. … The scrolls are carbonized by the heat, but also preserved. For centuries, as almost every other ancient text decays, the library of the Villa of the Papyri waits underground, intact.
F4.claim: in 79 AD the eruption buried a villa and its library under twenty meters of ash; the scrolls were carbonized and preserved, the library of the Villa of the Papyri intact underground
F4.lineage: the scrolls: the library of the Villa of the Papyri, carbonized in 79 AD

F5.quote: We can trace a scroll's surface, but where sheets are crushed or torn it still needs human help. Help us make it fully automatic.

F6.quote: We can see ink in some scrolls, but models trained on one rarely transfer to the next. Help us make them work on every scroll.

F6.lineage: the method's stated limits: human help, transfer, human input

F14.locus: The Role of the Vesuvius Challenge ¶1 (the card's snippet)
F14.quote: Launched in 2023, the Vesuvius Challenge transformed a long-standing scholarly problem into a global, open competition — mobilizing researchers, engineers and citizen scientists to do what had never been done before: read the Herculaneum scrolls without physically opening them.
F14.claim: launched in 2023, it made a long-standing scholarly problem into a global, open competition to read the Herculaneum scrolls without physically opening them
F14.lineage: what it is: an open science research organization and open competition reading the Herculaneum scrolls without unrolling them
F14.date: 2026-06-25 (the release, 'NAPLES, Italy (June 25, 2026)'); the page last updated 30 Sept. 2026

F15.locus: The Role of the Vesuvius Challenge ¶2
F15.quote: The initiative built on decades of work led by Seales — and a team of researchers with University of Kentucky’s EduceLab — who demonstrated machine learning could detect ink hidden within X-ray scans of carbonized papyri. With that proof of concept, Seales joined Silicon Valley leaders Nat Friedman and Daniel Gross to launch a $1 million global challenge aimed at accelerating progress.
F15.claim: it built on decades of work by Seales and EduceLab, who showed machine learning could detect ink in X-ray scans; Seales joined Nat Friedman and Daniel Gross to launch a $1 million global challenge

F16.quote: Following the successful extraction of characters from micro-CT X-ray imagery through the use of AI, Seales and co-founders Nat Friedman and Daniel Gross lauched The Vesuvius Challenge, a $1 million global competition to accelerate discoveries and read the scrolls. Seales’ team released software and thousands of 3D scans.
F16.claim: March 2023: Seales and co-founders Friedman and Gross launched it as a $1 million global competition; Seales' team released software and thousands of 3D scans
F16.date: 2023-03 (the timeline's entry; the page last updated 30 Sept. 2026)

F17.quote: Researchers confirmed that Herculaneum ink, made of carbon, is invisible in micro-CT scans. To address this, the team developed a neural network trained to detect subtle patterns associated with ink presence.
F17.claim: 2019: Herculaneum's carbon ink is invisible in micro-CT, so the team trained a neural network to detect patterns associated with ink
F17.lineage: the method: CT scanning, virtual unwrapping, machine-learning ink detection

F18.quote: The achievement establishes, for the first time, a scalable method for recovering complete texts from unopened scrolls — transforming a long-standing technical challenge into an active field of humanistic study.
F18.claim: the 2026 result establishes a scalable method for recovering complete texts from unopened scrolls

F19.quote: The Herculaneum papyri are more than 1,800 scrolls of papyrus discovered in the 18th century in the Villa of the Papyri in Herculaneum . They had been carbonized when the villa was engulfed by the eruption of Mount Vesuvius in 79 AD .
F19.claim: the Herculaneum papyri are more than 1,800 scrolls found in the 18th century in the Villa of the Papyri, carbonized in the eruption of 79 AD
F19.lineage: the scrolls: the library of the Villa of the Papyri, carbonized in 79 AD

F20.quote: In its current state, reading of the scrolls is extremely difficult and can risk destroying the information it holds. Techniques to decipher the writings on the scrolls are still being developed. For the first time, researchers recovered all the surviving text from a single scroll in 2026.
F20.claim: reading the scrolls is extremely difficult and risks destroying them; techniques are still being developed; in 2026 all the surviving text of a single scroll was recovered for the first time

F21.quote: This intense parching took place over an extremely short period of time, in a room deprived of oxygen, resulting in the scrolls' carbonization into compact and highly fragile blocks.
F21.claim: the parching carbonized the scrolls into compact and highly fragile blocks
F21.lineage: the scrolls: the library of the Villa of the Papyri, carbonized in 79 AD

F22.quote: Herculaneum papyri were written using a carbon-based ink, the chemical composition of which is extremely similar to that of the surrounding carbonized parchment.
F22.claim: their carbon-based ink is chemically extremely similar to the carbonized surface it is on, which defeats standard CT contrast
F22.lineage: the method: CT scanning, virtual unwrapping, machine-learning ink detection

F23.quote: In the same year, he demonstrated a readable unrolling of another Herculaneum scroll, with help of the particle accelerator Diamond Light Source ; through an X-ray imaging technique, ink containing trace amounts of lead was detected.
F23.claim: 2018: Seales demonstrated a readable unrolling of a Herculaneum scroll with the particle accelerator Diamond Light Source
F23.lineage: the method: CT scanning, virtual unwrapping, machine-learning ink detection

F24.quote: In 2023, Nat Friedman , Daniel Gross , and computer scientist Brent Seales announced the Vesuvius Challenge, a competition to "decipher Herculaneum scrolls using 3D X-ray software". … The Vesuvius Challenge offered a $700,000 grand prize to be awarded to the first team that could extract four passages of text from two intact scrolls using 3D X-ray scans.
F24.claim: Wikipedia: announced in 2023 by Nat Friedman, Daniel Gross and computer scientist Brent Seales as a competition to 'decipher Herculaneum scrolls using 3D X-ray software', with a $700,000 grand prize for four passages from two intact scrolls

F25.quote: On 12 October 2023, the project awarded $40,000 to Luke Farritor , a 21-year-old computer science student at the University of Nebraska, for successfully detecting the first word in an unopened scroll: porphyras
F25.claim: 12 October 2023: $40,000 to Luke Farritor for the first word detected in an unopened scroll, porphyras ('purple')
F25.lineage: milestones: the first word and the 2023 Grand Prize

F26.quote: On 5 February 2024, the project awarded its 2023 Grand Prize of $700,000 to the winning team and $50,000 each to three runner-up teams for successfully revealing 5% of one scroll , and announced its goal for 2024 of revealing 90% of the four scrolls that it has fully scanned. … The uncovered text is believed to be a previously unknown text of Philodemus , "centered on the pleasures of music and food and their effects on the senses".
F26.claim: 5 February 2024: the 2023 Grand Prize ($700,000) and three $50,000 runner-up prizes for revealing 5% of one scroll, believed a previously unknown text of Philodemus; the 2024 goal 90% of four scrolls
F26.lineage: milestones: the first word and the 2023 Grand Prize

F27.quote: In June 2026, the Vesuvius Challenge team announced that PHerc. 1667, known within the project as "Scroll 4", had been virtually unwrapped and read end-to-end. … A project preprint described the work as the first complete virtual unwrapping and extended reading of a rolled Herculaneum papyrus. In the PHerc. 1667, 22 columns of text were recovered, containing "a Stoic philosophical treatise that may be attributable to Chrysippus ".
F27.claim: June 2026: PHerc. 1667 ('Scroll 4') virtually unwrapped and read end to end, the first complete virtual unwrapping of a rolled Herculaneum papyrus; 22 columns of a Stoic treatise that may be attributable to Chrysippus

F28.quote: Besides PHerc. 1667, the team were able to read the title and author of PHerc. 139: Philodemus , On Gods, Book 8 .
F28.claim: the title and author of PHerc. 139 read: Philodemus, On Gods, Book 8

F29.quote: The Vesuvius Challenge is a machine learning, geometry and computer vision competition to read the Herculaneum Papyri.
F29.claim: its account on X defines it as a machine learning, geometry and computer vision competition to read the Herculaneum Papyri
F29.lineage: what it is: an open science research organization and open competition reading the Herculaneum scrolls without unrolling them

F34.quote: NAPLES, Italy (June 25, 2026) — The Vesuvius Challenge has achieved a historic breakthrough in the recovery of the Herculaneum scrolls — revealing new texts, titles and authors unknown to history and ushering in a new era for the study of the ancient world.
F34.claim: the University of Kentucky's release: a historic breakthrough, new texts, titles and authors unknown to history

F35.quote: Full virtual unwrapping of the surviving portion of PHerc. 1667 — revealing nearly 1.5 meters of text across 20 columns … Recovery of more than 70 columns of text from PHerc. 172, housed at Oxford’s Bodleian Library … Identification of completely new books from the ancient world by Epicurean philosopher Philodemus, including On Vices, Book 1 and On Gods, Book 8
F35.claim: PHerc. 1667 fully unwrapped, nearly 1.5 m across 20 columns; more than 70 columns from PHerc. 172 (Bodleian); new books of Philodemus, On Vices 1 and On Gods 8

F36.quote: “This scroll was deemed completely unreadable when part of it was opened in the 1980s,” Federica Nicolardi, assistant professor in papyrology at the Università degli Studi di Napoli Federico II, said. “While a few isolated letters were visible, overlapping layers obscured the writing, and the scroll was assigned a readability score of zero. But now, with virtual unwrapping, we can follow sustained arguments across multiple columns.
F36.claim: Nicolardi: PHerc. 1667, partly opened in the 1980s, was assigned a readability score of zero; with virtual unwrapping its arguments can be followed across columns

F37.quote: Nicolardi leads a team of Vesuvius Challenge papyrologists whose contributions are essential to both the creation of machine learning models and to the interpretation of text from the scrolls.
F37.claim: its papyrologists are essential both to making the machine-learning models and to interpreting the text
F37.lineage: after the machine: the papyrologists read

F38.quote: According to the papyrological team’s analysis, the text does appear to be a philosophical treatise concerned with ethics, arts and human behavior, likely reflecting Stoic thought. … “If this text had been found in Egypt or anywhere else, it would probably have been classified straight away as a Stoic text. The fact that it comes from a collection that is almost entirely Epicurean makes us more cautious in drawing conclusions,” Nicolardi added.
F38.claim: the papyrologists read a treatise on ethics, arts and human behavior, likely Stoic, and are cautious because the collection is almost entirely Epicurean

F39.locus: The Role of the Vesuvius Challenge ¶3
F39.quote: Through the competition, Seales’ team released open-source software and high-resolution 3D X-ray images from two intact scrolls and several fragments.
F39.claim: through the competition Seales' team released open-source software and 3D X-ray images of two intact scrolls and several fragments

F40.locus: The Role of the Vesuvius Challenge ¶6–7
F40.quote: Today, the Vesuvius Challenge has a dedicated team of researchers and technical experts who support contestants with preconditioned data, new tools and improved access to the scroll scans. … At its core, the Vesuvius Challenge has become more than a competition. It’s a collaborative effort to recover a lost library — powered by shared data, open innovation and a global community united by a common goal: bringing ancient voices back to life.
F40.claim: it now has a dedicated team supporting contestants, and has become more than a competition: a collaborative effort to recover a lost library
F40.lineage: what it is: an open science research organization and open competition reading the Herculaneum scrolls without unrolling them

F41.quote: As new texts are emerging faster than ever from the carbonized papyri, the focus is shifting from the engineers and computer scientists designing high-tech tools to the experienced papyrologists, classicists and historians who can interpret, contextualize and ultimately bring these ancient works back into human knowledge. … “This is no longer just about imaging or machine learning,” Seales said. “Now we need experts who can read, edit and understand what they are saying.”
F41.claim: the focus shifts from the engineers to the papyrologists, classicists and historians; Seales: 'Now we need experts who can read, edit and understand what they are saying'
F41.lineage: after the machine: the papyrologists read

F42.quote: More than 600 Herculaneum scrolls remain unopened.
F42.claim: more than 600 Herculaneum scrolls remain unopened
F42.lineage: the scrolls: the library of the Villa of the Papyri, carbonized in 79 AD

F43.quote: “For nearly two millennia, many of these texts have been physically preserved but intellectually inaccessible,” said Brent Seales, Vesuvius Challenge co-founder

F49.quote: $800,000 to the first team or individual to fully unroll and make readable a scroll from the set below. We also have prizes for second place ( $100,000 ) , third place ( $50,000 ) , and fourth place ( $50,000 ) — $1,000,000 in total.

F51.locus: General conditions; Compute and data conditions
F51.quote: It does not have to be open source at the time of submission, but you have to make it open source under a permissive license, publicly on GitHub, to accept the prize. … Any dataset created or used to train ML models must be published publicly, under a CC-BY-NC 4.0 license.
F51.claim: winners must open-source their code under a permissive licence and publish their training data under CC-BY-NC 4.0

F52.quote: The larger your model's window size, the easier it is for it to invent plausible letterforms instead of recovering real ink. Large windows are fine, but you must demonstrate that the text is not hallucinated
F52.claim: the larger an ink model's window, the easier it invents plausible letterforms; submissions must show the text is not hallucinated
F52.lineage: review, verification and the bar against hallucinated text

F53.quote: All submissions will be assessed by the Review Team, which consists of a Technical Team to review your methodology, and an independent Papyrology Team to review your results.
F53.claim: submissions are reviewed by a Technical Team (method) and an independent Papyrology Team (results)
F53.lineage: review, verification and the bar against hallucinated text

F54.quote: For these prizes, your mission is to prove that ink detection works on scrolls where nothing has been read yet. The review bar is deliberately high — we’d rather be slow than wrong. … First Letters prizes will be awarded for a maximum of 9 more scrolls — up to $450,000 in total.
F54.claim: First Letters prizes test ink detection where nothing has been read; 'we’d rather be slow than wrong'; up to $450,000 for at most 9 more scrolls
F54.lineage: review, verification and the bar against hallucinated text

F55.quote: We have already recovered the titles of PHerc. 172 and PHerc. 139 — but the title of Scroll 1, the scroll where the first passages were read, is still missing. … Scroll 1 is one of our most-read scrolls: substantial continuous Greek text of an Epicurean prose work has been recovered, yet its author and title remain unknown.
F55.claim: the titles of PHerc. 172 and PHerc. 139 are recovered; Scroll 1's Epicurean prose has author and title still unknown

F56.quote: If no team meets the criteria by the deadline, we reserve the right to award the prizes to the teams that came closest. This is not a guarantee … Prizes are awarded at the sole discretion of Scroll Prize, Inc. and are subject to review by our Technical Team, Annotation Team, and Papyrological Team.
